projects.name: AUREVAN Atlas 01
projects.short: A cinematic luxury watch commercial built entirely in AI, from macro dial detail to the movement inside the case.
projects.objective: Present a titanium automatic watch with the restraint and precision a luxury buyer expects, without a studio, a macro rig or a physical sample.
projects.description: A sixteen-second product film for the Atlas 01 automatic. Macro passes across the green sunburst dial, the exposed movement, the bracelet links and the full product on a lit pedestal, cut to a single rhythm.
projects.challenge: Luxury watch advertising is judged on detail. The dial finish, the bracelet geometry and the movement have to survive being held on screen, and any inconsistency between shots breaks the illusion that these are the same object. Macro product work at this level normally means a studio, a loupe lens and a real sample.
projects.solution: The piece was shot-planned like a conventional watch commercial — establishing turn, dial macro, movement reveal, bracelet detail, hero on pedestal — so the generated footage had a structure to sit inside rather than being assembled from whatever looked good. Branding, dial typography and the green-and-titanium palette were fixed before production so every shot reads as the same watch. The grade keeps shadows deep and highlights controlled, and the cut holds each macro just long enough to register.

projects.name: ANA Naturkosmetik
projects.short: A German-language natural skincare commercial built around ingredient storytelling and clean product photography.
projects.objective: Communicate a natural, clinical skincare range to a German-speaking audience, with the active ingredients made visible rather than described.
projects.description: A twenty-second product film for ANA Naturkosmetik covering serum, SPF 30 and body cream, with ingredient sequences for aloe, hyaluronic acid and botanical oils, closing on the brand mark.
projects.challenge: Natural skincare has a credibility problem: every brand claims the same botanicals. Saying 'hyaluron' does nothing; the audience has to see it behave like a serum. The range also had to read as premium and clinical at once, in German, without the language carrying the whole message.
projects.solution: Each active ingredient got its own visual beat — aloe leaves beside the bottle, a hyaluronic strand lifting from a pipette, botanicals suspended in liquid — so the claims are shown rather than stated. The palette holds to deep green and gold throughout, which keeps the three products reading as one range. German on-screen type was kept to single words at the moments where the visual already made the point.

projects.name: AZUREA Beach Club
projects.short: A cinematic brand film selling the feeling of a day at a Mediterranean beach club rather than its facilities.
projects.objective: Make a venue desirable by showing the experience of being there — the crowd, the light, the sound — instead of listing what it offers.
projects.description: A twenty-second brand film moving through a beach club day: pool and terrace, the DJ booth, dancing, golden-hour crowds, a drink in close-up, and the venue at blue hour.
projects.challenge: Hospitality venues are usually sold with wide shots of empty furniture, which communicates the space but none of the reason to go. The film had to feel full and alive, carry a time-of-day arc, and look like a single consistent venue rather than a montage of unrelated locations.
projects.solution: The edit follows one day rather than one tour: afternoon by the pool, the DJ taking over, the crowd building, sunset, then night. Keeping a consistent architecture, a linen-and-sand wardrobe palette and the same warm-to-blue light progression makes the generated footage read as one place. Handheld-style motion and shallow focus on the crowd shots keep it closer to documentary than to an advert.

projects.name: Never Stop Exploring — Concept Spec
projects.short: An unofficial concept commercial in the language of technical outdoor advertising — weather, endurance and gear under stress.
projects.objective: Demonstrate that AI production can carry a premium outdoor brand film: harsh weather, visible wear on the gear, and a single human story.
projects.description: A twenty-three second concept spot following one climber from forest approach to summit, with the jacket, pack and boots doing the storytelling.
projects.challenge: Outdoor brand films live on physical credibility — ice in a beard, mud on a boot, wind pulling at a hood. Generated footage tends toward the clean and the weightless, which is exactly wrong for this category. The piece also had to hold one recognisable character across changing locations and weather.
projects.solution: Wear and weather were treated as the subject rather than the backdrop: frost on the face, a scuffed boot sole on wet rock, a hood pulled against wind. Continuity on the yellow jacket, the pack and the climber's face anchors the sequence as one journey. Sparse on-screen lines carry the voice, and the edit builds from enclosed forest to exposed summit so the scale lands at the end.

projects.name: BMW i7 Frozen Edition — Concept Spec
projects.short: An unofficial concept car commercial built around a single idea: precision in any climate.
projects.objective: Show that a premium automotive spot — light-trail opening, speed, detail passes, hero shot — can be produced without a vehicle, a location or a camera car.
projects.description: A fifteen-second concept commercial opening on an illuminated grille rendered in light particles, moving through snow and ice driving footage, wheel and surface detail, and closing on a hero shot and endline.
projects.challenge: Car advertising is a genre with fixed expectations: the light-signature open, the speed sequence, the detail pass, the hero. Hitting those beats with generated footage means keeping one vehicle visually identical across radically different lighting — neon dark, blown-out snow, overcast ice — which is where consistency usually fails.
projects.solution: The spot was storyboarded against the conventional structure so each shot had a job. Vehicle colour, wheel design and proportions were locked as references before production. The cold grade runs through every shot, which both unifies the footage and carries the 'frozen edition' idea without stating it. The endline lands on a plain black card so the last thing on screen is the proposition.

projects.name: Big Thicc Cats — Panther
projects.short: A black-on-black jewellery film where liquid metal becomes a panther and the panther becomes the ring.
projects.objective: Give a sculptural panther ring an origin story rather than a product shot.
projects.description: A thirty-three second product film built on a single transformation: liquid metal forms a panther, the panther moves, and the form resolves into the finished ring with sapphire eyes.
projects.challenge: Jewellery this small is hard to make dramatic, and a black product on a black background gives almost nothing to light. A straight turntable would have shown the piece without giving anyone a reason to care, and the panther motif needed to feel earned rather than decorative.
projects.solution: The film leads with the metaphor and delivers the product last. Liquid metal, smoke and water carry the transformation, with specular highlights doing all the shape definition against the dark field — which is how black objects are lit in practice. Holding the reveal to the final seconds means the ring arrives with the panther's weight already attached to it.

projects.name: Beauty Circle — SQT Bio-Needling
projects.short: A vertical treatment ad that moves from skin concern to booked appointment in twenty seconds.
projects.objective: Turn a clinic treatment into a bookable offer on social, with the problem, the method, the outcome and the price all landing inside a feed-length cut.
projects.description: A twenty-second vertical ad for an SQT Bio-Needling treatment, opening on the skin concern, introducing the product system, demonstrating the device in use, and closing on price and a booking call to action.
projects.challenge: Aesthetic treatments are a considered purchase sold in an impulsive medium. The ad had to name the concern precisely enough that the right viewer recognises themselves, explain an unfamiliar method, and still reach a price and a call to action before the scroll — all in a calm register, because clinical anxiety sells nothing.
projects.solution: The structure does the work: a direct question as the hook, the product system shown as a considered object, the device demonstrated on skin, then the result shown as calm rather than dramatic. The palette stays cream, marble and soft daylight throughout, which reads as clinic rather than salon. Price and the booking line are held on screen at the end rather than flashed, so the offer is the last thing the viewer sees.
projects.resultsNote: Illustrative figures showing the scale of change this kind of creative is built to produce. Not measured results from this project.

projects.name: Bleame — UGC Ad Set
projects.short: A set of creator-style ads for a skincare tool, built for paid testing on TikTok and Facebook.
projects.objective: Produce multiple UGC-style variations of the same offer so a paid campaign has something to test against.
projects.description: A thirty-second UGC ad set for the Bleame exfoliating tool, built from spoken-to-camera hooks, demonstration footage, before-and-after comparison and a closing urgency line.
projects.challenge: Paid social needs volume: one ad is a guess, and creative fatigue sets in within days. Filming several creators for a single product is slow and expensive, and the format has to look unproduced — the moment it looks like an advert, performance drops.
projects.solution: Several distinct creator personas and hooks were produced for the same product so the campaign could test opening lines rather than whole concepts. Each follows the UGC grammar — handheld framing, domestic settings, caption-first delivery, the product held rather than displayed — with the demonstration and the comparison shot carrying the proof. All cuts are captioned for sound-off viewing and exported vertical for both platforms.

projects.name: AI UGC Skincare Ad Set
projects.short: A reel of creator-style skincare ads across several products, hooks and presenter types.
projects.objective: Show the range of UGC approaches available for skincare — problem-led, review-led, routine-led — within one body of work.
projects.description: A fifty-second compilation of UGC-style skincare advertising: spoken-to-camera openings, product-in-hand reviews, application sequences and mask and patch demonstrations across several presenters.
projects.challenge: Skincare is the most crowded category on paid social, and viewers have learned to recognise and skip the formats. Each variation needed a genuinely different entry point rather than the same ad with a new face, and the claims had to stay general enough to survive platform review.
projects.solution: The set works through distinct openings — a problem named out loud, a sceptical review, a question about a condition — each paired with the presenter type that suits it. Application and texture footage provides the proof in place of claims. Captions carry every hook so the ads work muted, and each is framed and exported for vertical placements.

projects.name: 21st Century Mega Multi
projects.short: A creator-style supplement ad delivered by a presenter in a clinical setting.
projects.objective: Give a multivitamin a credible, conversational recommendation in a UGC format.
projects.description: A forty-five second vertical UGC ad for a multivitamin, delivered to camera in a hospital corridor and office setting, built on an energy-and-routine narrative with captions throughout.
projects.challenge: Supplements are a low-trust category sold on personal recommendation, so the ad had to sound like someone talking rather than a brand claiming. It also had to hold attention for forty-five seconds of talking head, which is long for a feed.
projects.solution: The script is structured as a personal routine rather than a product pitch — how the day feels, where the product fits — with the bottle held up only once the claim has been made conversationally. Setting changes between corridor and desk break up the talking head and give the cut some rhythm. Animated keyword captions highlight one phrase at a time to keep the eye moving.

projects.name: AI Influencer — Podcast Format
projects.short: A two-minute podcast-style talking head built for clipping into short-form content.
projects.objective: Produce long-form presenter content in a podcast setting that can be cut into many short vertical clips.
projects.description: A two-minute vertical video in a podcast set — warm lighting, microphone, plants, studio chair — with a presenter discussing skincare and collagen, captioned throughout with keyword highlighting.
projects.challenge: Short-form content is expensive to produce one clip at a time. The podcast format is the standard solution because a single session yields dozens of clips, but it only works if the set, the lighting and the presenter stay consistent enough that every clip looks like part of the same series.
projects.solution: A fixed set and framing were established so the format is repeatable: the same chair, lighting, microphone and background across the whole runtime. The script is written in self-contained segments, each of which stands alone as a clip, so cuts can be taken anywhere without losing the thread. Keyword-highlighted captions run throughout, which is what makes the clips readable muted.

projects.name: Apex 18 Golf Lounge
projects.short: A 3D animated pitch video selling a corporate golf lounge concept to investors and members.
projects.objective: Explain a hospitality concept — what it is, who it is for and why it works commercially — in a format that holds a room.
projects.description: A ninety-second 3D animated pitch video following characters through an Apex 18 venue: arrival, simulator bays, the boardroom and the lounge, with on-screen ROI metrics.
projects.challenge: A venue that does not exist yet cannot be filmed, and architectural renders do not show how a space is used. The pitch had to communicate the business model alongside the atmosphere, and hold attention for ninety seconds in front of an investor audience.
projects.solution: Animated characters walk the viewer through the space in the order a member would experience it, so the layout is understood without a floor plan. Business content is placed where it belongs in the story — the boardroom scene carries the ROI metrics — rather than being bolted on as a slide. The stylised 3D look sidesteps the uncanny quality of photoreal interiors and keeps the tone warm.

projects.name: Slimpur Compression Suit
projects.short: A 3D animated transformation ad for a compression garment, built on a character arc rather than a product demo.
projects.objective: Sell a body-worn product by showing the change in how the wearer carries himself.
projects.description: A fifty-eight second 3D animated vertical ad following a character from self-consciousness through wearing the garment to visible confidence, closing on product detail and branding.
projects.challenge: Body-product advertising is sensitive territory: it has to acknowledge the viewer's concern without shaming them, and it has to show a change without the before state reading as cruel. A straight product demonstration would have shown the garment and sold nothing.
projects.solution: The story is told through posture and behaviour rather than physique — hiding under a hoodie at the start, open and upright at the end — which keeps the emotional arc intact without dwelling on the body. The stylised animation keeps it from feeling like a real person being judged. Product construction detail is held to the end, after the reason to care has been established.

projects.name: Claymation Brand Film
projects.short: A character-led animated brand film built on warmth, childhood and family moments.
projects.objective: Carry a brand on feeling alone, with no product on screen and no voiceover claims.
projects.description: A thirty-second animated brand film in a soft 3D claymation style, moving through vignettes — a puppy and a rabbit, a child riding, friends playing, a parent embracing children, winter lights.
projects.challenge: Emotional brand films fail when the sentiment is generic. Each vignette had to land in two or three seconds and connect to the next, and the character style had to stay consistent across completely different settings, which is where generated animation usually breaks.
projects.solution: A fixed character design language — proportions, eye style, surface finish — was established first so every vignette reads as the same world. The sequence builds outward from animals to children to family to a shared moment, which gives the film a direction rather than being a series of nice scenes. The warm, slightly matte look does the emotional work in place of dialogue.

projects.name: Eight Senses — Mushroom Cacao
projects.short: A 3D character animation that turns functional mushrooms into cast members for a German-language product ad.
projects.objective: Make a functional mushroom supplement approachable and memorable for a German-speaking audience.
projects.description: A thirty-three second vertical animated ad for a mushroom cacao blend, with each mushroom variety animated as a character in its own environment, resolving to the product and a discount offer.
projects.challenge: Functional mushroom supplements have an image problem — the ingredient is unfamiliar and faintly medicinal, and the category is full of earnest wellness language. The ad had to make lion's mane, reishi and chaga feel friendly rather than clinical, and still arrive at a concrete offer.
projects.solution: Each mushroom was given a character and a habitat matched to its benefit — a reading room for focus, a track for energy, a forest pool for calm — so the varieties are distinguishable without a word of explanation. The product arrives in a real domestic setting after the characters have done their work, and the German offer card closes it with the discount stated plainly.

projects.name: AI Commercial & Product Reel
projects.short: A showreel cutting across the product, automotive, lifestyle and cinematic work into one sequence.
projects.objective: Give a prospective client a single piece that demonstrates range, finish and the kinds of work available.
projects.description: A forty-one second reel moving through lifestyle, sport, automotive, jewellery and cinematic landscape footage, with captioned copy carrying the proposition over the top.
projects.challenge: A showreel has to establish quality in the first two seconds and hold it, with no story to carry the viewer. Cutting between unrelated categories risks looking like a collection of samples rather than a body of work with a point of view.
projects.solution: The reel is cut to the copy rather than the other way round, so each line of on-screen text lands on the shot that proves it. Pacing accelerates through the middle and opens out on the final landscape shot. A consistent grade across very different source material is what makes the sequence read as one body of work.

projects.name: AMIGOS — 5 Minutes To Goodness
projects.short: A 3D animated quick-service food commercial built around a five-minute countdown.
projects.objective: Give a fast-food promise — five minutes to a finished order — a visual device that makes it concrete.
projects.description: A twenty-six second 3D animated commercial following an order from counter to hand, with an on-screen countdown clock running from 5:00 to 0:00 across the build.
projects.challenge: Speed claims in food advertising are abstract until they are shown. The spot also had to make the food itself appetising in an animated style, which is harder than photoreal food footage because the viewer has no reference for the texture.
projects.solution: The countdown clock appears in every scene and does the structural work, turning the build sequence into a timer the viewer is watching. Food shots are lit and framed like live-action food photography — steam, close focus, condiment detail — rather than like animation. The payoff lands on the clock reaching zero with the finished order in hand.

projects.name: Adult Care — Healthcare Avatar
projects.short: A presenter-led explainer for adult care services, delivered by an AI avatar in a care setting.
projects.objective: Explain an adult care service in a calm, person-to-person register rather than a corporate one.
projects.description: A sixteen-second vertical avatar video delivered to camera in a care office setting, with a care schedule and nursing reference material in frame.
projects.challenge: Care services are chosen at a stressful moment, usually by a family member rather than the person receiving care. The tone has to be reassuring and plain, and the setting has to look like somewhere care is actually organised rather than a stock office.
projects.solution: A single presenter delivers the whole message to camera with no cuts, which is the right choice for reassurance — movement and editing would undercut it. The set dresses the role rather than the brand: a visible care schedule, nursing references on the shelf, warm domestic lighting. Pacing is deliberately unhurried.

projects.name: First Light Coffee
projects.short: A cinematic coffee commercial that treats the morning cup as the turning point of a city waking up.
projects.objective: Sell a coffee brand on atmosphere and ritual rather than on beans, roast notes or price.
projects.description: A thirty-three second commercial moving from an empty blue-hour city through commuters arriving, into the shop, and closing on espresso pouring into the cup.
projects.challenge: Coffee advertising is saturated with the same two shots: the pour and the steaming mug. The piece needed a reason to watch past the first second, and had to hold one consistent city, one consistent shop and recognisable faces across a full narrative arc rather than a montage.
projects.solution: The spot is built as a short film rather than an advert — the city is established empty and cold first, so the warmth of the shop lands as relief. Characters recur across shots, which is what makes it read as one morning rather than stock footage. The grade runs cold blue outside and warm amber inside, and the espresso pour is held to the last beat as the payoff the whole film has been building toward.

projects.name: FORMA Performance Footwear
projects.short: A performance running shoe commercial built on motion, effort and sole detail.
projects.objective: Show a running shoe doing the thing it is built for, and finish on the product clean enough to shop from.
projects.description: A twenty-second commercial following a runner from lacing up through strides, stair work and a golden-hour run, closing on a studio product shot of the shoe.
projects.challenge: Performance footwear is sold on feel, which is invisible. The ad had to make cushioning and grip legible through motion alone, and keep one shoe design consistent through fast action before resolving to a clean studio shot that matches it exactly.
projects.solution: Low angles and foot-level framing put the sole and the midsole geometry on screen during the action, which is where the technology actually shows. Shot lengths shorten as the run builds, then stop dead on the static product shot — the change in rhythm is what makes the final frame land. The shoe's colourway and sole structure were locked as references so the studio shot reads as the same product.

projects.name: Eighty Eight Footwear
projects.short: A lifestyle footwear commercial following one pair of shoes through a full day in the city.
projects.objective: Position a comfort shoe as something worn everywhere rather than for one activity.
projects.description: A sixty-second commercial tracking the product through street, library, commute and errands, with the brand mark present throughout and a logo animation close.
projects.challenge: Comfort footwear has no dramatic hook — it is a product defined by the absence of discomfort. The ad had to build a case through accumulation rather than one big moment, and keep a consistent shoe design across many settings and both colourways.
projects.solution: The structure is cumulative: each scene is a different context, same shoes, and the argument builds by repetition rather than by claim. Framing stays low and close on the feet so the product is never off screen for long. A persistent brand bug keeps attribution present through a long runtime, and the logo animation gives the piece a defined end rather than a fade.

projects.name: Fashion E-Commerce Product Video
projects.short: A clean studio product video replacing a model shoot for an e-commerce listing.
projects.objective: Give an online listing the turnaround, drape and detail footage a shopper needs before buying.
projects.description: A fifteen-second studio video presenting a knit and trouser look on a model: front, three-quarter, back, fabric drape and footwear detail.
projects.challenge: E-commerce product video has a fixed job — show fit, drape and detail from every angle on a neutral background — and no room for interpretation. Garment construction has to stay identical across every angle, which is exactly where generated footage normally drifts.
projects.solution: The video follows the standard e-commerce grammar deliberately: full look, rotation, back, then detail passes on the fabric fall and the shoe. A flat grey cyclorama and even lighting keep attention on the garment and make the footage drop into a product page without clashing. Seam placement, colour and silhouette were fixed as references so the garment is the same item in every shot.

projects.name: Colour Pairing Lookbook
projects.short: A styling video built as a series of colour pairings, each one a shoppable look.
projects.objective: Turn a clothing range into styling advice so the content is useful rather than promotional.
projects.description: A seventeen-second vertical video presenting six colour pairings — light blue and white, navy, cream and sage, red and grey, teal and cream, teal and camel — each as two complete styled looks side by side.
projects.challenge: Lookbook content gets scrolled past because it shows clothes without telling anyone what to do with them. The format also had to deliver six distinct pairings in seventeen seconds without becoming a blur, and keep a consistent studio and model treatment so the range reads as one collection.
projects.solution: Framing each pairing as a named colour combination turns the content into advice — the viewer gets a rule they can use, and the clothes come with it. Two looks per frame doubles the information per second without extra time. The identical wardrobe setting, poses and accessories across all six mean the eye only registers what changes, which is the colour.

projects.name: Fashion FPV Drone Reel
projects.short: An FPV-style fashion reel where the camera move is the edit.
projects.objective: Give a fashion look the energy of a drone-led shoot without a drone, a location permit or a crew.
projects.description: A sixteen-second vertical reel built on FPV camera movement — orbiting and diving around a model on the steps of a colonial-style building, with speed-ramped transitions.
projects.challenge: FPV work lives or dies on the movement feeling physically possible. Generated footage tends to drift or float in ways a real drone cannot, which breaks the effect instantly, and transitions between passes have to hide the joins rather than advertise them.
projects.solution: Camera moves were kept to paths a real FPV pilot could fly — committed arcs and dives with consistent momentum, not floating. Motion-blur transitions are placed at the fastest part of each move, where the eye cannot resolve detail, so the cuts disappear. Cutting to the music rather than to the footage keeps the reel driving through its full length.

projects.name: Chewlax Cooling Mat
projects.short: An animated pet-product ad that tells the story from the dog's side first.
projects.objective: Sell a pet cooling mat to owners by showing the problem through the animal rather than the specification.
projects.description: A fifty-seven second animated vertical ad following a dog lying on a cold tile floor, its owner noticing, the product introduced with a cutaway of the gel layers, and the pair outdoors together at the end.
projects.challenge: Pet products are bought on guilt and affection, not features, but the mat still has to be explained — a cooling gel layer means nothing unless the viewer sees how it works. Animation also had to carry emotion without an animal looking uncanny.
projects.solution: The ad opens on the dog alone on hard tile, which states the problem without a word, and only then brings in the owner noticing — the emotional beat the purchase actually turns on. The gel construction is explained with a clean exploded cutaway placed after the viewer already cares. The closing garden scene pays off the opening image: the same pair, comfortable. Large word-at-a-time captions carry it muted.

projects.name: Children's Sleepwear UGC Ad
projects.short: A parent-voiced UGC ad for a children's pyjama set, framed as a bedtime routine.
projects.objective: Sell a children's clothing product through a routine a parent recognises rather than a product description.
projects.description: A thirty-eight second vertical UGC ad opening on a parent at bedtime, moving through the garment in hand, fabric and stitch detail, the set worn, and closing on a caption block with the product details and handle.
projects.challenge: Children's clothing is bought on fabric, safety and wash durability — details that need to be seen up close — but the ad still had to feel like a parent sharing something rather than a brand selling. Balancing the close product detail against the domestic warmth is where this format usually tips one way or the other.
projects.solution: The ad is structured around the routine: a time stamp on screen sets the scene, the garment is handled the way a parent actually handles it, and only then does the camera go close on the cotton and the stitching. Specification appears as a caption chip rather than a voiceover claim. The closing text block carries the full detail for anyone who watched to the end.

projects.name: BrimBaby Wedding Story
projects.short: A 3D animated family story centred on a West African wedding, told from a child's point of view.
projects.objective: Carry a brand on a family story with real cultural specificity rather than a generic animated family.
projects.description: A sixty-nine second animated story moving from a family at home through a traditional wedding ceremony, the celebration, and back to the family together.
projects.challenge: Culturally specific animation fails when the detail is approximate — gele tying, agbada draping, the aso-ebi palette all have to be right or the audience it is made for disengages immediately. The story also had to hold for over a minute with characters consistent across a dozen scenes.
projects.solution: The cultural detail was treated as the point rather than set dressing: the headwrap, the embroidery, the ceremony staging and the kente upholstery at home all carry weight. Character designs were fixed first so the family stays recognisable from the opening scene to the last. The structure returns deliberately to where it started, which gives a long piece a shape instead of a sequence of nice moments.

projects.name: Family Storytelling Animation
projects.short: A 3D animated short about a father coming home, built to carry a brand message through family warmth.
projects.objective: Tell a complete emotional story in thirty seconds with no dialogue the viewer has to follow.
projects.description: A thirty-second animated piece following a father arriving home, a family moment on the sofa, reading together, and a walk at sunset.

projects.objective: Build trust for a home-services company by showing the whole chain of response, not just the van arriving.
projects.description: A storm hits, a thermostat stops responding and a homeowner is left standing at the wall. The ad follows the call through a dispatcher, out to a technician on the rooftop unit, and back to the homeowner's relief, closing on the fleet and the crew at golden hour.
projects.challenge: Emergency home-services advertising is usually a phone number over a stock truck. The brief needed the viewer to believe there is an actual organisation behind the number, within half a minute and without naming a single named employee or a real address.
projects.solution: The ad is structured as a relay — homeowner, dispatcher, technician, homeowner again — so competence is demonstrated by the handoffs rather than claimed in copy. The resolution is played on the customer's face instead of the repaired unit, because that is what the audience is actually buying. The closing fleet shot establishes scale without making a numerical claim the company would have to stand behind.

projects.name: First Impressions Matter
projects.short: A 24-second before-and-after film taking a tired commercial building through preparation and repaint to a finished facade.
projects.objective: Sell commercial repainting as a property investment rather than a maintenance cost, by showing the change rather than describing it.
projects.description: The film opens on a weathered, stained building under flat grey light and moves through the work itself — sheeting, scaffold, prep, brushwork — before arriving at the finished facade under a clear sky. Four lines carry the argument: first impressions matter, preparation makes the difference, skilled workmanship and fresh perspective, and a coat of paint can make a real change.
projects.challenge: Before-and-after is the oldest device in contractor marketing and the easiest to disbelieve. Two photos prove nothing, because viewers assume the angle, the light or the building changed. The film had to make the transformation credible and give weight to the preparation work, which is where the cost actually sits and which clients routinely undervalue.
projects.solution: The before and after are framed from the same position so the comparison is anchored to one viewpoint and the change cannot be read as a different building. The middle third is given entirely to preparation — sheeting, scaffold, masking, the brush on the surface — because that is the part being sold. Light carries the emotional arc from overcast to clear, and the copy stays short enough to read on a phone with the sound off.

projects.name: You Scanned 200 Badges
projects.short: A 43-second landscape ad about the conference leads that go cold, and the automated follow-up that catches them.
projects.objective: Sell automated lead follow-up to exhibitors by naming the specific moment the value is lost — the week after the show.
projects.description: The ad opens on a trade-show floor with a question: you scanned two hundred badges at the show, how many will you follow up? It then shows the alternative working — replied in seconds, booked, reminded, they show up, no quote goes quiet — with the SMS thread on screen, and closes on an offer to book a fifteen-minute demo.
projects.challenge: Exhibitors know follow-up matters, so an ad that simply says so adds nothing. The piece had to locate the failure precisely enough that the buyer recognises their own last event in it, and then show the product working in a format that reads at desktop scale without becoming a screen recording.
projects.solution: The hook is a number and a question rather than a claim, which makes the viewer do the arithmetic on their own stack of unworked badges. The product is then demonstrated as a sequence of outcomes — replied, booked, reminded, attended — so each beat answers a separate objection. Phone interfaces are composed large and held against clean backgrounds, and the ask is a short demo rather than a purchase.

projects.name: Gwinnett Home Services
projects.short: A 54-second explainer walking a homeowner from a broken air conditioner to a confirmed contractor booking through a local directory.
projects.objective: Show homeowners how the directory works end to end, so the first visit feels familiar rather than unfamiliar.
projects.description: A homeowner stands at a failed outdoor unit. The film moves into the product — browsing home service pros in Gwinnett County, filtering by trade, comparing listed providers, filling the contact form — and back out to the same homeowner on the phone with contact details confirmed. It closes on the brand line: local help for the place you call home.
projects.challenge: Directory products are judged in the first ten seconds and are hard to make interesting, because the experience is mostly reading and clicking. The explainer had to hold attention through genuine interface walkthroughs while keeping small screen text legible, and had to keep the emotional frame — a homeowner with a problem — from disappearing into the UI.
projects.solution: The piece is bookended by the homeowner so the product sits inside a human problem rather than replacing it. Interface sections are cut to the decisions a user actually makes — pick a trade, compare, contact — and each screen is held only as long as its one decision needs, with the active element scaled up so it reads in a feed. The resolution is the confirmation, not the submission, because the thing being sold is the reply.

projects.name: VELARA — Own The Moment
projects.short: A 29-second dark-luxury fragrance commercial built from gold smoke, liquid and light around a single bottle.
projects.objective: Give a fragrance concept the visual register of a luxury house film, where nothing is explained and everything is suggested.
projects.description: A faceted bottle sits in near-darkness as gold smoke and liquid move around it. Four lines arrive and leave — a scent beyond ordinary, depth character presence, leave an impression, own the moment — before the brand lockup resolves and the bottle returns, lit, for the final frame.
projects.challenge: Fragrance cannot be shown, only implied, so the entire burden falls on texture, movement and light. At 29 seconds with no narrative and no cast, the risk is a sequence of attractive but unrelated shots that never accumulates into a brand.
projects.solution: A single visual vocabulary was fixed first — gold, black, smoke, liquid, faceted glass — and every shot drawn from it, so the piece reads as one object seen many ways rather than a reel. The bottle is kept as the constant that each abstract passage returns to, which is what turns atmosphere into branding. Copy is set sparse and widely tracked to sit inside the image rather than on top of it, and the lockup is held last so the name lands on the strongest frame.
